title: Case study: train booking rush
objective: Survive a booking rush: never sell a seat twice, release seats held by people who leave, and keep the database alive when booking opens.

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017), chapter 7: preventing lost updates
Cloudflare Docs: Waiting Room (queues surges of visitors so they don't overload the origin)

simplifies: IRCTC is named only for context; this is not its architecture, and nothing here describes its systems (its site couldn't be reached to check anything). Seat counts, database capacity, payment times and the 10× rush are illustrative. Real booking also has seat classes, quotas, waitlists and payment failures.

challenges.title: One seat, one passenger
challenges.prompt: Booking reads the free-seat count, then writes it back minus one. Keep seats sold twice at zero the whole time for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: Two buyers read "40 seats free" at the same moment, and both write back 39. What went wrong?

options.text: Two seats were sold, but the count only went down by one
options.explanation: Right. That is a lost update: one buyer's write overwrote the other's.
Both got seats, but the count now says one more seat is free than really is.
Nothing refuses it; each write looks fine on its own.

challenges.hint: What if checking for a free seat and taking it happened in one step?
challenges.explain: An atomic "take a seat if one is free" (a conditional update in the database) can't interleave with another buyer's, so the count never goes wrong.

challenges.title: People who leave
challenges.prompt: 60% of buyers leave without paying, and their seats are held for 60 seconds. Keep seats held by people who left at 180 or fewer for 10 seconds.
challenges.hint: Each held seat waits until its hold runs out. How long should that be?
challenges.explain: Shorter holds return unpaid seats to sale sooner. Too short, and real buyers lose their seat mid-payment: holds are a trade-off.

challenges.title: Booking opens
challenges.prompt: At 2 seconds, booking opens and 10× the buyers arrive for 5 seconds. Keep failed bookings at 1% or less the whole time for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: The database handles 200 bookings a second and 400 a second arrive. What happens to the rest?

options.text: They fail: requests time out at the overloaded database
options.explanation: Right. Past its capacity, the database can't serve them.
Past capacity, the queue grows without limit until requests time out.
Adding capacity takes time; the rush lasts seconds.

challenges.hint: What if buyers queued before reaching the database, and were let in at a rate it can handle?
challenges.explain: A waiting room admits buyers at a safe rate. Nobody gets an error, but look at the waiting time: the rush becomes a queue instead of a crash.

critique.prompt: A proposal for the booking site: no waiting room; booking reads the free count and writes it back minus one; seats are held until the buyer pays, however long that takes.

risks.text: Read-then-write can sell one seat to two passengers
risks.why: Two bookings that interleave both see the same count; use one atomic conditional update.

risks.text: Holds never expire, so seats of people who left are never released
risks.why: Give holds a short expiry, so unpaid seats go back on sale.

risks.text: When booking opens, the rush goes straight to the database
risks.why: A waiting room admits buyers at a rate the database can handle.

risks.text: Buyers must sign in before booking
risks.why: Normal for ticketing (names on tickets, limits per person); not a design flaw.
A feature; it reads availability, which the fixes above keep correct.

critique.hint: Think about two buyers at once, buyers who leave, and the moment booking opens.

options.text: Make taking a seat atomic: two passengers with one seat is the worst outcome
options.explanation: Right. It breaks the system's core promise and can't be undone at the station.
Crucial for the rush, but errors can be retried; a double-sold seat can't.
It loses sales, but no one is promised a seat that doesn't exist.

critique.explain: Correctness first (one seat, one passenger), then availability under the rush (waiting room), then efficiency (expiring holds). Each fix trades something: atomic updates add database work, waiting rooms add waiting, short holds risk timing out slow payers.

quiz.prompt: Why does "read the free count, then write count − 1" sell seats twice?

options.text: Two buyers can read the same count before either writes, so both take the last seat
options.explanation: Right. That's a lost update; an atomic conditional update prevents it.

options.text: Seat counts are stored as text
options.explanation: The type isn't the problem; the two separate steps are.

quiz.prompt: What does a waiting room trade?

options.text: Buyers wait longer, but the database stays within its capacity and nobody gets errors
options.explanation: Right. A queue instead of a crash.

options.text: It sells more seats than exist
options.explanation: It changes when buyers arrive, not how many seats there are.
